title: Why is Kafka so fast
sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Design (https://kafka.apache.org/40/design/design/): throughput of hard drives has diverged from seek latency; random writes far slower than linear; 'using the filesystem and relying on pagecache is superior to maintaining an in-memory cache'; all data is 'immediately written to a persistent log on the filesystem without necessarily flushing to disk'; two common inefficiencies are 'too many small I/O operations, and excessive byte copying'; protocol built around a 'message set' abstraction that groups messages; with sendfile the OS sends data 'from pagecache to the network directly'; 'efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together rather than compressing each message individually'.

Illustration only: the size meter, message chips and the copy path in the zero-copy shot are simplified drawings, not measurements. 'Check your durability settings' is a practical summary of the 'without necessarily flushing' point, not a quote.

lines.text: Kafka writes every message to disk, and yet it handles huge streams, so why is it so fast?
First, it only appends to the end of a log, and sequential writes are far faster than random ones.
Second, it leans on the operating system's page cache, instead of building its own cache.
Third, it batches messages together, so the cost of small requests is shared.
Fourth, it compresses whole batches, which works far better than one message at a time.
And with zero-copy, the operating system sends data from the page cache straight to the network.
But here's the catch: writes aren't necessarily flushed to disk right away, so check your durability settings.
lines.caps: BUT THERE IS A *CATCH | NOT *FLUSHED RIGHT AWAY | CHECK *DURABILITY

lines.text: So Kafka is fast because it works with the disk and the OS, so append, batch, and skip the copies.
